Agreed, I like "matrix" more than "ragged_matrix".

>

Also happy with this change. Writing the former felt wrong.

> I don't think we want to get in the habit of defining N x 1
> or 1 x N matrices since they'll behave like matrices, not
> like vectors.  And I absolutely don't want to coerce one into

Right now my plan is to handle naming in RStan rather than in the Stan code. I believe there's a way to specify names in the print function. The more general the Stan code, the less often it'll need to be compiled.

Good point. But for homogenously sized arrays of matrices currently
matrix[rows,cols] X[shelves]
it is accessed by shelf, row, and column. That is confusing, but we should be consistenly confusing.

> How would you feel about using just matrix[rows,cols] instead
> of "ragged_matrix"?  I really don't like "ragged_matrix", because
> the matrix isn't itself ragged.

Agree. A matrix is a matrix.

> Also, I'd strongly prefer
>
>   vector[cols] beta[K];
>
> to

> by indexing rather than by name.  But your mileage may vary.  And
> I see the problem with big ones either way --- with arrays you
> have to keep some kind of symbol table mapping from indexes to
> names, whereas with names, you have what looks like duplicated code.

Part of the reason for doing this is to auto-generate Stan code or to use Stan code that can be compiled once at install time. We can figure out the naming on the (R for the near term) interface side but we need to be able to write abstract code on the Stan side.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Writer refactor
messages.body_plain:
Allen,

Okay, everything is merged and tests passing and ready for you
to give it a shot at feature/issue-1361-writer_callback.

You should be able to reduce a bunch of code by using the
new method services, as in the now much shorter
src/stan/services/command.hpp.

I believe you’ve already implemented an interrupt callback, which
just means you’ll have to implement writer callbacks for info, errors,
algorithm output, and algorithm diagnostics.  info and errors can
just point to cout/cerr (see src/stan/interface_callbacks/writer/(cout|cerr).hpp)
but if you want to guarantee absolutely silent output you can also add
switches and other fancy accouterments.  I think you can have some fun
with the output and diagnostic writers — the key/value callbacks should
allow you to write useful items directly into Python memory (like the
adapted step size and metric, plus all the timings) while the std::vector
callback should allow you to stream the samples somewhere useful
as they come in.

Anyways, let me know what you think.

-Mike

messages.subject: Automated Diagnostics
messages.body_plain:
I whipped up an example of automated diagnostics that you can try out
at https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/tree/feature/automated_diagnostics.

Any opinions on the text?  It’s meant to be informative but make no hard
decision about the validity of the output (as theoretically we cannot do
that).  The user will have to have a basic understanding of a Markov
chain — eventually we can reference the appropriate review section
in the manual.

Any diagnostics I’m missing?

(keeping bin/print agnostic to validity) or should we roll it together into
one single analysis executable?

messages.subject: Re: retranslating BUGS models to Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I think the models should run on either JAGS or WinBUGS and I would actually recommend using WinBUGS.

JAGS 3.4.0 is not able to deterministically lay out the DAG in the memory which leads to different results even when the input is exactly the same. You must be very careful when you ask for exact reproducibility with JAGS. Only in some situations the output from JAGS becomes exactly reproducible! JAGS 4.0.0 is supposed to solve this issue. Of course, statistical wise everything is fine.

Concerning importance: The suggestion from Aki sounds great, i.e. give it with guidelines to students... getting a stiff ODE solver into Stan is hopefully the number one prio...

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Comments on Command Refactor
messages.body_plain:
One advantage to using double* is that it can generally be passed without requiring a memory copy.  If a call requires std::vector<double> and you have anything *except* that type, you will need to allocate more memory and make a copy in order to make the call.  Using std::vector<double> for the API pretty much ensures that this happens for almost any call that interfaces between R/Matlab/Python/etc and Stan.  While not a huge performance hit for typical models now, if we are serious about scaling to big datasets, it's something to consider.

Cheers,
Marcus

dealing with an Eigen matrix that has a .data() method. Whereas
everything that supports wrapping C++ already knows about

currently work in any event (e.g., var_context uses vector<double>).

other software (Julia, etc.) it seems like sticking to just C++11 is a

messages.body_plain:
This is, by the way, the reason I originally used vector<double> instead
of Eigen --- it's just more portable to other interfaces.

Yes, memory is contiguous for vector<double>, but not vector<vector<double> >.

Marcus is absolutely right that there's no way to create a vector<double> from
a double* without copying, even in C++11, because vector<double> wants to manage
the memory.   That's the main advantage of using it over a double* (other than
that you also don't have to keep passing lengths around).  See:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/vector/vector/vector/

Yes, we can copy a vector<double> to another without a deep copy using move
semantics in C++11.  Or swap as Rob points out.

To avoid copying a vector<double>, can't we pass by reference, or by
pointer as a last resort?  Or we can manage memory using a vector<double>
and pass a reference to the memory, but this is dangerous, as resizing
can cause the contents to move.  That is, a vector<double> is guaranteed
to have contiguous memory at any given time, but that location is just
a handle, not a hard reference, so it may move.

We can't create a MatrixXd in Eigen without a copy, but we can use
the Map<MatrixXd> expression template to do the copy lazily or not
at all depending on how it's used.

- Bob

> On Apr 2, 2015, at 6:12 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Marcus, this is what the move constructors will accomplish.  Once we move to C++11
> then we can use whichever type we want (double*, std::vector, Eigen::Matrix) and
> translate between them with no copy or allocation cost.  Right now we can hack
> around this by using &v[0] and assuming that the implementation is contiguous memory
> of the right size without any sneaky alignment tricks.

>> From what I understand, I don't think the move constructor actually makes a difference here, as it only works if you're creating from an existing std::vector. Please correct me if I'm wrong though.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Comments on Command Refactor
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 2, 2015, at 12:04 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>
> If it's only a vector<double> you can use Map<MatrixXd> to map it onto
> an Eigen matrix without a copy.

Map<MatrixXd> is an expression template that wraps raw data.
As soon as it's assigned, there's a copy implicated.  So if you do this:

  Map<MatrixXd> y(...);
  MatrixXd m <- y;

you get a copy.  If you just use it in something like an addition,
you can sometimes avoid the copy.

> It's the vector<vector<double>> that's
> the problem (and a big one, since that's how RStan and PyStan hold their
> chains).

OK --- that decisions on the RStan and PyStan side.

> Is there any C++11 way to create a vector<vector<double>> that is
> contiguous?

No.  A vector<double> manages its memory independently on the heap.

You need to use an array.  Or use the Boost Array package to do it
more generally.

> Can we use an std::array or something? If there was a way to
> do this cleanly, RStan and PyStan could use Stan's ess and rhat
> routines.

std::array is C++11, I'm afraid.  It also doesn't do anything for you
other than template out the size so the size is static, which you
don't want.

I don't see anything for you other than to malloc your own 2D array
structure.  I'd suggest doing it following std::vector so it uses
the RAII pattern in C++ and thus will ensure memory safety.

- Bob

On Wednesday, April 1, 2015 at 7:48:09 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Can you set the seed for JAGS?  If not, I wouldn't expect
> to get the same answers twice in a row.  I also don't know
> how to do that for WinBUGS.   I never used either of those
> pieces of software to do more than fit a couple models.
>
> - Bob

Yes, there are variables called ".RNG.seed" and ".RNG.name" which can be used to control the random variables, and if using R, both rjags and runjags allow you to pass values to JAGS in the initialization as well.

For example using runjags, you can set inits as such:

inits <- function(chain) {list(alpha.prior = 20 + rnorm(2, 0, 1), theta.prior = 1000 + rnorm(2, 0, 10), m = sample(c(1, 2, 3), size = 1, prob=c(.8, .15, .05)), .RNG.seed = chain ^ 2 + 1, .RNG.name = "base::Mersenne-Twister")}

messages.subject: revised ragged array spec
messages.body_plain:
It dawned on me that if we're introducing ragged arrays,
then we can use them to declare ragged arrays.

I added a general example-driven spec to the top of the
doc Rob started:

messages.body_plain:
The first part of what Andrew wants (almost) works now, using

  data = globalenv()

in the call.  I suppose the RStan devs could make that the default,
then Andrew would get to do exactly what he wants.

I believe it will fail if there are certain things in the global
environment that RStan can't deal with in terms of reading them as data.

I'm not an R expert, but I'm thinking if RStan would define the var_context
to pull from the global environment as variables are needed, then this
caveat could be removed.

The second thing Andrew wants also (almost) works, but not as is.
You need to define a new environment, with the global as default
parent, then assign in that new environment and pass it in.

> sigma <- 4
> e <- new.env()
> e$mu <- 2

Then if you use data=e, you will get mu = 2 and sigma = 4.

And again, I see now reason why rS couldn't give An exactly what
he wants.

Now whether it should is another matter.  Using globals this way is
dangerous because junk lying around in the environment will be
inadvertently brought in and used to define data accidentally.  Also,
any scripts using this technique will likely be completely non-reproducible
by the next person because they'll forget to include the data definitions.

I'd personally rather encourage hygienic and reproducible programming
habits.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:

> On Apr 4, 2015, at 12:08 PM, Jiqiang Guo <guo...@gmail.com> wrote:

Right --- there's no function to get it.  I could add something
static to provide names and dimensions, but sizes are dynamic.
But I don't think that's needed here.

> And passing .GlobalEnv by default is not a good idea since there is a preprocess of the data, which needs to check all the NA/NaN in the data and set data to integer types if there is no loss of precision.

Thanks for explaining what can go wrong here.

Is there no way to make the var_context implementation do all this work lazily
rather than building it all up in memory ahead of time?

I think there are two advantages:

1.  no duplication of data, and

2.  no problems with extraneous variables passed in possibly being undefined
    or having NaN or NA values.

It should be possible because the constructor for the generated program
class will attempt to pull each item out of the var_context.  At the
point the constructor tries to pull the data values from the var_context,
it tells the var_context what the sizes are.

It would require a custom implementation of var_context on the R side that
knows how to read from an R environment.  Then if you passed in variable
definitions (e.g., list(a=3, b=c(1,23)), the values would go in the environment.

- Bob

messages.subject: Editing Wiki
messages.body_plain:
I ran 'grep' on the Stan unit tests looking for EXPECT_ and ASSERT_ an put together a short list of commonly used tests with links to the GoogleTest doc so it's less bewildering for someone who needs to write tests.  I was going to put this into the Stan Wiki on using GoogleTest. but I think I don't have permission to edit the wiki.

#### Common test types:

The documentation (above) is excellent so check there for details but here is a directory of commonly used test types in Stan:

* [EXPECT/ASSERT](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/Primer#Assertions) EXPECT records the result but allows further tests in the same function, ASSERT exits the current function without cleanup. Stan unit tests use both forms.
* [EXPECT_TRUE](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/Primer#Basic_Assertions) EXPECT_TRUE/FALSE test that the condition is TRUE/FALSE.
* [EXPECT_EQ](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/Primer#Binary_Comparison) Tests that a calculated value equals (==) an expected result exactly, not appropriate for floating point comparison.
* [EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/AdvancedGuide#Floating-Point_Comparison) Tests that a floating point calculation results to known output values.
* [EXPECT_NEAR](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/AdvancedGuide#Floating-Point_Macros) Like EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ but a third argument sets the threshold used.
* [ASSERT_THROW](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/AdvancedGuide#Exception_Assertions) Tests that a specific exception type is thrown.
* [ASSERT_NO_THROW](https://code.google.com/p/googletest/wiki/AdvancedGuide#Exception_Assertions) Tests that the statement does not throw. Some parts of the code are not supposed to throw... not sure which.

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 4, 2015, at 2:15 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> OK, now let me give the user’s perspective.

I understand that everything you're saying is from your
perspective as a user.  And partly my objection is not to
Andrew's feature request, but to R's scoping rules and how
they're used interactively.

R's scoping lets a function's scope grab variables out of
containing environments, as in:

> f <- function(x) { x + zzz; }

> f(3)
Error in f(3) : object 'zzz' not found

> zzz <- 12

> f(3)

[1] 15

Because R is interpreted, people (myself included, I'm ashamed
to admit) often use it interactively to define variables on the fly,
rather than running everything out of a script in a clean environment.
RStudio explicitly supports this by making it easy to evaluate fragments
of a program in the global environment.  Other users cut-and-paste, or
use the history with slight edits.

Putting R's scoping and interactive cut-and-paste-and-update together
leads to the non-reproducibility issues I'm worried about.

The only way to combat this of which I'm aware is to run everything
out of a script file in a clean environment.  If a program works that
way, it's good to go (assuming any data it reads is distributed along
with the script).

Now onto Andrew's preferred programming practice with RStan.

Do you (Andrew) always work by first defining every variable in
the Stan data block in the environment from which you call stan()?
Do you think that's what we should be encouraging everyone to do?
It's not what I tend to do, but I may very well be an outlier.

If so, then I agree that following the R2WinBUGS idiom of
forcing users to type data = list(a=a, b=b,...) is redundant.
I wouldn't call it "horrible", though, because it's the standard
way of calling functions in R and following the idioms of a language
makes programs more readable.  Specifying all the data variables
explicitly makes it clear what's getting passed in.  Neither of these are
intrinsically bad.

The introduction of data = c("a", "b", ...) was meant to cut
down on typing in the situation where variables are all defined
in the calling environment.

Jonah's nlist() function goes even further and has the useful
property that you can provide partial overrides, defining some
variables in the call and grabbing the rest from the environment.

> First, data=globalenv() is confusing for me.  I don’t necessarily want stan() to use the _global_ environment.  I want it to use whatever environment I’m calling it from. If I’m calling Stan from a function, or from a loop, or whatever, I’d like it to use whatever R would be using, and I’d like that to be the default.  This would perhaps deal with Ben’s objection.

Calling with data = environment() would use the current environment.
This cuts down typing even further and avoids having to enumerate the
names of the variables in the Stan program, which I know Andrew's objected
to before on many occasions.

Then, if environment() is the default value for data, Andrew gets exactly
what he wants, right?

The only problem is that it won't work now if the environment isn't
clean.  That's a positive in my mind, but then I'm a neat freak who
wants everyone to be a tidy programmer and not leave their dirty
variables (laundry) lying around in the environment (on the floor).
I think requiring a clean environment may be a dealbreaker for Andrew,
which is why I brought up a way to read data more lazily and make sure
only the variables in the Stan program get read out of the
environment (right now, everything from the environment is converted
to input and if any of them have NaN or NA you get an error, and if
any have string data, you get warnings).

None of these steps cuts down on my concern about the scope of R and
the habit of interactively updating environments.  In fact, I think
it encourages what I take to be dangerous programming practices.

But hey, that's just me and I realize I'm a worry wart and a neat freak.

> Second, I want to encourage hygienic and reproducible programming habits too.  And the current way it’s done is _not_ “hygenic and reproducible.”  The current approach is I have to read the data block in the Stan program, then retype them all as data in the stan() call, thus data(list(y=y,N=N,…)).  That’s super unhygenic because it copies code.  It means that when I change my Stan program I need to change the call, it’s horrible.

Could you give an example of the before and after Stan program and
what the environment looks like that works for both?  I don't understand
what you'd like to be able to do and how reading out of the current
environment would support it.

Now for what I want as a user.  I'd like to read a dump file into a list
then call stan() with that list as data.  I don't know how to do that
in R, though.  This would make it easy to use R data + program across
Stan interfaces and would ensure that everything's neatly reproducible.
At least assuming you check the latest script and data into version control
and tag which version is used to generate the data for a paper or whatever.

- Bob

Bob, you mean like this?

setwd(‘/path/to/current/directory')
data <- read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
fit <- stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)

You can do the same thing in PyStan, too,

data = pystan.read_rdump(‘data/model.stan.data')
fit = pystan.stan(file=‘model.stan', data=data, …)

This is how I work with the interfaces because it allows
me to use the same common data file.

I have to admit that I am incredibly opposed to having the entire
environment be the default, if only because then the mailing list
will be full of people sending scripts of failing models that we
can’t run because the environment is different.  Retyping may
lead to the occasional typo, but at least that typo will be the
same for everyone so we can readily diagnose it!

messages.body_plain:
There's something to be said for symbolic differentiation or
at least reusing the tape for autodiff.  It's less flexible
but potentially faster.  To really exploit the symbolic
representations for optimization is going to take a lot of lines
of code, though :-)

I don't see how lines of code for an interface is a reasonable
measure of anything, though.  And if you really wanted to count,
I'm not even sure what you'd do given that PyStan depends on
Stan which depends on Eigen and Boost and presumably PyMC3 depends
on Theano and NumPy.

What's the status of PyMC3?  The README.md at

  https://github.com/pymc-devs/pymc3

says:

  PyMC 3 is alpha software and is not ready for use in production.
  We encourage most new users to use the current release version in the
  PyMC 2 repository.

It would be worthwhile to evaluate it for expressiveness and
speed vs. PyStan once it's stable.  Or maybe even before it's stable.

messages.subject: Best practices...
messages.body_snippet:
Related to the discussion of best practices for translating BUGS models, I'll start asking questions

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol1/stacks/stacks_a_normal.s

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Best practices...
messages.body_plain:
OK, here's why I think this isn't going to be so easy.

First, keep in mind that what's best practice for efficiency
isn't the same as what's best practice for clarity.  Which
are we aiming for?  How direct should the translations of the
BUGS models be?

I was originally suggesting

 * a line-by-line very direct translation
 * a conversion of that to one using the priors, etc. we like,
   possibly rearranging data structures for efficiency, etc.
 * an efficient version of the good model
 * optionally an efficient version of the direct translation

The best practices on arrays vs. matrices are in the
manual chapter on arrays vs. matrices, so I suppose the
duplication of effort can begin by shoveling that chapter
into the best practices Wiki.

Then there's the advice to always use matrix functions
and shorter functions like elementwise functions if
you can to shorten the code.

But then given that this is just the transformed data
block, the vectorization and so forth aren't that important
since they only get executed once.  There's a section in the
manual on execution that's important to read to understand when
to put things in transformed data, transformed parameters, and
generated quantities.

Best practice is to always declare things as transformed data or
generated quantities if possible, always delcare things as local
variables if possible.  Lots of users inadvertently make everything
a transformed parameter or local variable in the model that should
be transformed data or a generated quantity.  So this all needs
to go in the best practices.

Another best practice is to use capital letters for
constants and then matching lower-case letters for loops.
This won't match BUGS, so I'm not sure where that goes
in the best practices vs. translation of BUGS models.
And follow Gelman et al. in variable naming, so no capital
letters like  Y.

Are mean_x and sd_x used elsewhere?  If not,
best practicses would dictate they be local variables.
This is so that their memory doesn't linger past when
they're used.  I see they are, but this should be mentioned
as a best practice if we're making a list.

We also need best practices for formatting.  I'm tired of
reading crazily formatted user models --- there's an appendix
to the manual for that.

Now onto the show.

On Apr 8, 2015, at 12:48 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> Related to the discussion of best practices for translating BUGS models, I'll start asking questions
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol1/stacks/stacks_a_normal.stan
> has
> ---clip---
> // to standardize the x's
> transformed data {
>  matrix[N,p] z;
>  row_vector[p] mean_x;
>  real sd_x[p];
>  for (j in 1:p) {
>    mean_x[j] <- mean(col(x,j));
>    sd_x[j] <- sd(col(x,j));
>    for (i in 1:N)
>      z[i,j] <- (x[i,j] - mean_x[j]) / sd_x[j];
>  }
> }

So I'd suggest this:

matrix[N,M] x;

transformed data {
  matrix[N,M] z;
  vector[M] mean_x;
  vector[M] sd_x;
  for (m in 1:M) {
    mean_x[m] <- mean(col(x,m));
    sd_x[m] <- mean(col(x,m));
  }
  for (n in 1:N)
    z[n] <- (x[n] - mean_x) ./ sd_x;
}

But maybe that ./ is too complicated to read?
Or maybe people don't like z[n] referring to a row
of a matrix?

This isn't ideal for speed, since the col(x,m)
operations have to copy.  So you can make a local

   col_x_m <- col(x,m)

to reuse it. A critical piece of best practices is
to define expressions only once and reuse them --- it's very
important for efficiency, but can make things harder to read.

And then you want to rearrange and the z[n] assignments are
not memory local, so aren't efficient for large matrices.  But
then there's a tradeoff with wanting to be able to define mu
with a matrix operation.  Also, do we really need to define
mu and sigma as transformed parameters?  It's overhead in writing
and in print and whatnot.  If not, use this:

  y ~ normal(beta0 + z * beta, sqrt(sigma_sq));

I like the "_" to separate words in names, but your mileage may
vary.

So many pieces of advice!

For the rest of that model, we don't ever really want to
be using step functions --- relational operators are much clearer, so
I'd rewrite

  outlier_3  <- step(fabs((Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma) - 2.5);

as

  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma - 2.5 > 0

or better still

  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma > 2.5

or even better for efficiency (multiplication is faster than
division),

  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) > 2.5 * sigma;

Best practice is not to include parens around things where the
language knows how to parameterize.  One might be tempted to
write ... > (2.5 * sigma).

Of course, rather than writing the same thing three times
with cut-and-paste, best practice would dictate writing
a function and actually declaring the booleans properly as
constrained integers.  First the function.

int is_outlier(double y, double mu, double sigma) {
  return fabs(y - mu) > 2.5 * sigma;
}

Then declare outlier_3, etc. as int<lower=0,upper=1>.
Best practice is to always have bounds for error checking and
self-documenting code.

Also for Andrew, random variables are not capitalized, so our
best practice notation is to use lower-case y.

Of course, Andrew doesn't like those priors, so then there's
the step of actually making the priors better and stating
best practices for those.  There's a bunch of advice extracted
from Andrew in the regression chapter of the manual.  But it's
quite involved and varies based on whether you're doing MCMC or
optimization.

Also, this

  for (j in 1:p)

    b[j] <- beta[j] / sd_x[j];

should be rewritten as:

  b <- beta ./ sd_x;

But then you see why you want row vectors vs. vectors
so that you can do all the matrix algebra with minimal
transpositions.  With mean_x being a row vector and b being
a vector, (mean_x * b) is a dot product.  Or you can use dot_product(a,b),
which is more efficient than making mean_x a vector and using
mean_x' * b (tranpose makes a copy).

Is BUGS (best practice spelling!) really taking

 beta ~ normal(0, 1e5)?

If so, we want full precision, so the exact translation
should be:

  beta ~ normal(0, sqrt(1e5));

or to eliminate the sqrt operation without losing precision,
either define a transformed data variable or use this

  beta ~ normal(0, 316.227766016838);

I prefer 1e5 to 100000, so I think scientific notation should
be a best practice if we're drilling down to that level.

- Bob

> ---clip---
>
> I think mean_x and sd_x should be same type. Which is better, and why row_vector and not vector? It's not affecting the performance, but it's just confusing now.
>

I've put some of that into StataStan (it was Ben's suggestion really) but only as an option, so you can type matrices(all) and get, errr... all the matrices. But it won't do it unless you type (all). We could add that for variables in the current data file too.

My reason for being a little wary was confidentiality of data. Someone might get upset at having accidentally published their Stan data, containing some sensitive information that they hadn't meant to release.

messages.subject: StataStan (alpha-test) on GitHub
messages.body_plain:
I finally got StataStan onto GitHub, as an alpha-test branch. A lot of time got consumed around Easter trying to get Windows to play nicely with it, so I'd really appreciate some unforgiving testing on Mac and other Windows / Linux versions.

Next, I'm going to do a proper comparison with the logic of the other interfaces, to adopt any good ideas. If you spot something that can make it more consistent, that would be helpful too. Anyone who doesn't use Stata is welcome to just email me an idea and I'll try to translate it.

And btw Stata's newly released v14 includes a Gibbs sampler and Metropolis-Hastings (spotted by Ben G), although the specification of a novel model is not simple (it basically builds on their MLE commands). I don't know what their longer-term strategy is for that.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Best practices...
messages.body_plain:
Hi, there are 2 issues:

1.  Translation of Bugs/Jags models to Stan.  I don’t think we need a line by line translation.  I think what is best is, for each model, for us to give the Stan equivalent, but changing anything that’s bad practice and explaining the changes in comments (for example, we don’t do inv-gamma(.001,.001) because of Gelman, 2006, and explaining how we set up the mixture model following the recommendations of the Stan manual, and explaining why we use normal(0,10) priors rather than normal with sd 1000.  A line by line translation would be fine but I don’t think it’s necessary, and it does represent effort, it represents effort that could better be used elsewhere, I think.

Regarding this translation, I think we should use what you (Bob) consider best practice in every case.  Including naming of variables (for example, n=1,…,N rather than i=1,…,n).  I mean, we don’t have to kill ourselves.  If the model’s already done we can leave it as is.  But if we have the option, if we’re choosing what to do, I I’d say let’s do what Bob would do.

2.  A wiki for best practices in Bayes and Stan.  For this, ambiguity is ok.  It’s fine that what’s best practice for efficiency isn’t the same as what’s best practice for clarity (and that clarity is in the eye of the beholder).  We can explain these things in the wiki.

A

> On Apr 7, 2015, at 11:56 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> OK, here's why I think this isn't going to be so easy.
>
> First, keep in mind that what's best practice for efficiency
> isn't the same as what's best practice for clarity.  Which
> are we aiming for?  How direct should the translations of the
> BUGS models be?
>
> I was originally suggesting
>
> * a line-by-line very direct translation
> * a conversion of that to one using the priors, etc. we like,
>   possibly rearranging data structures for efficiency, etc.
> * an efficient version of the good model
> * optionally an efficient version of the direct translation
>
> The best practices on arrays vs. matrices are in the
> manual chapter on arrays vs. matrices, so I suppose the
> duplication of effort can begin by shoveling that chapter
> into the best practices Wiki.
>
> Then there's the advice to always use matrix functions
> and shorter functions like elementwise functions if
> you can to shorten the code.
>
> But then given that this is just the transformed data
> block, the vectorization and so forth aren't that important
> since they only get executed once.  There's a section in the
> manual on execution that's important to read to understand when
> to put things in transformed data, transformed parameters, and
> generated quantities.
>
> Best practice is to always declare things as transformed data or
> generated quantities if possible, always delcare things as local
> variables if possible.  Lots of users inadvertently make everything
> a transformed parameter or local variable in the model that should
> be transformed data or a generated quantity.  So this all needs
> to go in the best practices.
>
> Another best practice is to use capital letters for
> constants and then matching lower-case letters for loops.
> This won't match BUGS, so I'm not sure where that goes
> in the best practices vs. translation of BUGS models.
> And follow Gelman et al. in variable naming, so no capital
> letters like  Y.
>
> Are mean_x and sd_x used elsewhere?  If not,
> best practicses would dictate they be local variables.
> This is so that their memory doesn't linger past when
> they're used.  I see they are, but this should be mentioned
> as a best practice if we're making a list.
>
> We also need best practices for formatting.  I'm tired of
> reading crazily formatted user models --- there's an appendix
> to the manual for that.
>
> Now onto the show.
>
> On Apr 8, 2015, at 12:48 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>>
>> Related to the discussion of best practices for translating BUGS models, I'll start asking questions
>>
>> https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol1/stacks/stacks_a_normal.stan
>> has
>> ---clip---
>> // to standardize the x's
>> transformed data {
>> matrix[N,p] z;
>> row_vector[p] mean_x;
>> real sd_x[p];
>> for (j in 1:p) {
>>   mean_x[j] <- mean(col(x,j));
>>   sd_x[j] <- sd(col(x,j));
>>   for (i in 1:N)
>>     z[i,j] <- (x[i,j] - mean_x[j]) / sd_x[j];
>> }
>> }
>
> So I'd suggest this:
>
> matrix[N,M] x;
>
> transformed data {
>  matrix[N,M] z;
>  vector[M] mean_x;
>  vector[M] sd_x;
>  for (m in 1:M) {
>    mean_x[m] <- mean(col(x,m));
>    sd_x[m] <- mean(col(x,m));
>  }
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    z[n] <- (x[n] - mean_x) ./ sd_x;
> }
>
> But maybe that ./ is too complicated to read?
> Or maybe people don't like z[n] referring to a row
> of a matrix?
>
> This isn't ideal for speed, since the col(x,m)
> operations have to copy.  So you can make a local
>
>   col_x_m <- col(x,m)
>
> to reuse it. A critical piece of best practices is
> to define expressions only once and reuse them --- it's very
> important for efficiency, but can make things harder to read.
>
> And then you want to rearrange and the z[n] assignments are
> not memory local, so aren't efficient for large matrices.  But
> then there's a tradeoff with wanting to be able to define mu
> with a matrix operation.  Also, do we really need to define
> mu and sigma as transformed parameters?  It's overhead in writing
> and in print and whatnot.  If not, use this:
>
>  y ~ normal(beta0 + z * beta, sqrt(sigma_sq));
>
> I like the "_" to separate words in names, but your mileage may
> vary.
>
> So many pieces of advice!
>
> For the rest of that model, we don't ever really want to
> be using step functions --- relational operators are much clearer, so
> I'd rewrite
>
>  outlier_3  <- step(fabs((Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma) - 2.5);
>
> as
>
>  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma - 2.5 > 0
>
> or better still
>
>  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) / sigma > 2.5
>
> or even better for efficiency (multiplication is faster than
> division),
>
>  outlier_3 <- fabs(Y[3] - mu[3]) > 2.5 * sigma;
>
> Best practice is not to include parens around things where the
> language knows how to parameterize.  One might be tempted to
> write ... > (2.5 * sigma).
>
> Of course, rather than writing the same thing three times
> with cut-and-paste, best practice would dictate writing
> a function and actually declaring the booleans properly as
> constrained integers.  First the function.
>
> int is_outlier(double y, double mu, double sigma) {
>  return fabs(y - mu) > 2.5 * sigma;
> }
>
> Then declare outlier_3, etc. as int<lower=0,upper=1>.
> Best practice is to always have bounds for error checking and
> self-documenting code.
>
> Also for Andrew, random variables are not capitalized, so our
> best practice notation is to use lower-case y.
>
> Of course, Andrew doesn't like those priors, so then there's
> the step of actually making the priors better and stating
> best practices for those.  There's a bunch of advice extracted
> from Andrew in the regression chapter of the manual.  But it's
> quite involved and varies based on whether you're doing MCMC or
> optimization.
>
> Also, this
>
>  for (j in 1:p)
>    b[j] <- beta[j] / sd_x[j];
>
> should be rewritten as:
>
>  b <- beta ./ sd_x;
>
> But then you see why you want row vectors vs. vectors
> so that you can do all the matrix algebra with minimal
> transpositions.  With mean_x being a row vector and b being
> a vector, (mean_x * b) is a dot product.  Or you can use dot_product(a,b),
> which is more efficient than making mean_x a vector and using
> mean_x' * b (tranpose makes a copy).
>
> Is BUGS (best practice spelling!) really taking
>
> beta ~ normal(0, 1e5)?
>
> If so, we want full precision, so the exact translation
> should be:
>
>  beta ~ normal(0, sqrt(1e5));
>
> or to eliminate the sqrt operation without losing precision,
> either define a transformed data variable or use this
>
>  beta ~ normal(0, 316.227766016838);
>
> I prefer 1e5 to 100000, so I think scientific notation should
> be a best practice if we're drilling down to that level.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
>> ---clip---
>>
>> I think mean_x and sd_x should be same type. Which is better, and why row_vector and not vector? It's not affecting the performance, but it's just confusing now.
>>
>> Aki
>>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Best practices...
messages.body_plain:
The point was that Sebastian (and others) were asking for
us to translate

   *** the exact same model ***

into Stan so that

  *** they could compare the results are the same. ***

That would specifically entail

  *** not changing the priors.  ***

A secondary goal was just helping people learn how to code
in Stan by translating the BUGS models they already know and
love in the simplest possible way.

We know

  * Michael has a bunch of issues with any such comparisons
    from a statistical computation point of view (e.g., tail
    probabilities and ergodicity),

  * Andrew has a bunch of issues with doing this from a statistical
    methodology and modeling point of view (e.g., priors), and

  * I have a bunch of issues with doing this from a Stan programming
    point of view (e.g., local variables).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] StataStan (alpha-test) on GitHub
messages.body_plain:
Well, we know Gibbs and Metropolis don't work very well for
complicated models compared to HMC/NUTS, so no worries we'll
be made redundant.

I wouldn't worry initially about merging modeling syntaxes.

In particular, I'm dead set on the idea of the Stan modeling
language being the same across platforms.  What we could
eventually do is provide a "simpler" language that translates
to the Stan language --- Ben already has something like that
going for the lme4 or glm language of R.

- Bob

> That's interesting. They have written a Gibbs and M-H sampler with a limited range of distributions. I suspect it will run faster than BUGS/JAGS by virtue of their speedy matrix language Mata,

Where's the matrix processing?  Are the models going to be
interpreted or compiled?

The usual bottleneck for random-walk M-H is the density
evaluation and the usual bottleneck for Gibbs is the conditional
sampling.  Neither of these involve matrices except for some
multivariate things, and for that, JAGS at least uses the
R libs, which are themselves based on fast underlying matrix ops.

- Bob

to be the "official set of Stan models"?

as long as we put big warning labels on them with directions on where
to find the recommended alternatives.  If we do decide to distribute
direct translations ("official" or not), you and Sebastian will have
to negotiate how strong to make those warnings --- he made the compelling
point that we didn't want to offend BUGS users, but gradually bring lure
into the fold.

I see the advantages and disadvantages of both including them and
not including them and honestly don't care one way or the other.  So I'm
going to bow out and let other people try to arrive at a final policy.

- Bob

messages.subject: massive doc reargue?
messages.body_plain:
I'm concerned about duplicated effort if we start focusing
on a best practices Wiki.

The manual now has roughly 5 components

I.    Programming Guide
      Chapters 1 - 21, Appendices B, C
      225 pages

II.   Language Specification
      Chapters 22 - 28, parts of 54, 55, Appendix D
      100 pages

III.  Built-in Function Guide
      Chapters 29 - 35
      125 pages

III.  Bayes, MLE, and MCMC
      Chapters 52 - 54
      25 pages

IV.   Algorithms
      Chapters 56, 57, 58
      15 pages

V.    Software Process
      Chapter 59
      10 pages

There's also an appendix on licensing and a bibliography.

 * Michael wants to rewrite Algorithms

 * Andrew wants to restart the programming guide as a Wiki

 * We can break out the process as a separate doc a la R

 * The manual can then be reduced to just the language spec
   and functions

 * We can just scrap the intro to Bayes and MLE (though it'd
   be nice to have something free to distribute as an alternative
   to always telling people to buy BDA)

- Bob

I agree that we don’t want to propagate bad models, but if we
were really serious about that then we wouldn’t be showing many
BUGS models at all!  The problem is that people want to use
these translations to _learn_ the Stan modeling language and

from BUGS into Stan.  The _only_ way we’ll be able to have

code improvements.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Best practices...
messages.body_plain:
I think the current BUGS example models are quite direct translations, and we don't need to repeat that. Just let them be there and add warning that they don't follow the best practices and meant only for people familiar with BUGS/JAGS.

I'm teaching Stan to people who have never used BUGS or gamma priors, and I don't want to spend time explaining the wrong models. That's why I'm willing to spend my time to add BUGS derived "data analysis examples" using the best practices in Stan. I wrote "data analysis examples", implying that we can make also other changes than just prior changes. For example, I could add log_lik computation for LOO for all models where it's applicable. Data analysis examples in BUGS example volumes are nice because they are small and have already the back story written, but also include many types of hierarchical models.

Aki

messages.subject: calling Stan from R
messages.body_plain:
Hi, there was a discussion recently about using global or local environments in the Stan call.  I tried running stan() with the argument data=.GlobalEnv but it didn’t run so I must have been doing something wrong.  (I actually wanted to specify the local environment but I couldn’t remember what it was called.)

Also, the question came up as to why I wanted to do this.  Ben recommended that I write my Stan functions more generically (with variables such as x,y rather than income,vote or whatever).  Even so, things can get messy.  For example, from something I happen to be working on right now:

fit1 <- stan("extrap_impsampling.stan”, data=c("J","T","J_prime","T_prime","y","y_prime_bar","x","x_prime","mu_delta_p","Sigma_delta_p","mu_delta_g","Sigma_delta_g","J_tilde","K"), iter=1000, chains=4, seed=0)

Keeping all these parameters in the data list, it’s just bookkeeping and a waste of time.  This is an example of where it would help to just pass the local environment.

A

> Wait, you’re kidding, right??  This is more lines of code than simply doing data=c(“J”,”T”,…)!

I presumed you were creating the environment to swap things in and out calling stan() a bunch of times. If you were only calling stan() once, then I wouldn't do it my way. I guess you could do it in 2 lines

fit1_env <- new.env()
invisible(sapply(c("J", ..., "K"), FUN = function(x) assign(x, get(x), envir = fit1_env)))

Since no one has objected to me putting something like this inside sampling(), optimizing(), etc., I guess we can do it.

parse_data <- function(program, e = parent.frame()) {
  cppcode <- scan(what = character(), sep = "\n", quiet = TRUE,
                  text = stanc(program)$cppcode)
  private <- grep("^private:", cppcode) + 1L
  public <- grep("^public:", cppcode) - 1L
  # pull out object names from the data block
  objects <- gsub("^.* ([0-9A-Za-z_]+).*;.*$", "\\1",
                  cppcode[private:public])
  # get them from the calling environment
  mget(objects, envir = e, inherits = TRUE,
       ifnotfound = vector("list", length(objects)))
}

Ben

the environment manipulation, but that's not an issue.
Assuming it does the right thing with arrays and vectors
and all the data types and isn't whitespace sensitive

name mangling at which point this is likely to fail and
have to be updated.

model API, but then somebody would have to do
the code generation for that, and Andrew's brought this up

messages.subject_clean: new web site w. new logo and color scheme
messages.body_plain:
Has anyone other than me and Michael had a chance to
check out Michael's new web site design?  It's in
the stan-web repo on the new_logo branch.

It features the new logo.  I modified the style a wee
bit from where Michael had it to make the h2 headers
darker and to extend the width of the header.

What I'd really like to figure out is how to set it
up so the nav and logo were on the left.   The advantage
of the right is that it doesn't disrupt reading the current
page --- the advantage of the left is that it doesn't float
off screen or get too far away.

There's also the issue of whether we release the new logo now
or wait for Stan 3.

Michael also set up a UK-based Stan store for swag, which
would be nice to link into the web site Shop page.   Which
brings up the question of whether we should remove the original
logo t-shirts or leave them there for nostalgia sake?  Maybe
if we pixelize or distress them to make them look even more retro
so people can wear them ironically?

- Bob

On Friday, April 10, 2015 at 9:55:57 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I would prefer a solution that actually queried the model
> for variable names which we could make part of the stable
> model API, but then somebody would have to do
> the code generation for that, and Andrew's brought this up
> so many times I know he doesn't want to wait.

Yeah, that would be better but the C++ code is pretty easy to grep for the names of the object in the data block. This just creates a list of objects by searching through the stack of R environments for objects that have the same names as objects in the data block of the Stan program. From there, the behavior would be the same as if the user had passed such a list to stan().

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sampling from final variational approximation
messages.body_plain:
We need that for MLE and MML, too.  The one you want to
coordinate with is Rob Trangucci, who's in charge of the MLE
and MML efforts.

The code should probably go somewhere more general than in
with VB, like in the model utility class.

I'm happy to chime in on design, but it should be relatively
simple.  We have the multi_normal_rng function already defined.
And the transform is available through the generated model code,
though it's not pretty to use standalone.

What we really need to do is change the model, which currently
uses the method write_array to convert the array of unconstrained
parameters to an array of constrained parameters.  Then there
are methods to pull out the parameter names and sizes/dimesnions
in the order they're generated by the model.  Just be careful to
keep in mind it's last-index major (column major for matrices).

- Bob

using multi_normal_rng().   There are examples of just this in the GP
section of the manual.

Is it possible to do even better somehow by rescaling uniform(0,1) variates
directly?  I know you can do inverse CDFs, but that's unlikely to be a
computational win over normal_rng() or Boost would've implemented normal
RNGs that way.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan's custom matrix multiply() slower than Eigen operator*
messages.subject_clean: Stan's custom matrix multiply() slower than Eigen operator*
messages.body_plain:
I've been doing some careful evaluations for the paper on Stan's
autodiff and realized that for two matrices of type Matrix<var, Dynamic, Dynamic>,
that Eigen's built-in operator*(a,b) is about 50% faster for autodiff
than Stan's custom stan::agrad::multiply(a,b) function!

I'm attaching plots of time taken relative to Stan for pretty much all
the other open-source, operator overloading C++ autodiff packages and
for just calling the functions with double arguments.

didn't work, so there's an order dependency there.

#include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>

then it works.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan's custom matrix multiply() slower than Eigen operator*
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Stan's custom matrix multiply() slower than Eigen operator*
messages.body_plain:
Hmmm, strange.  This definitely goes against our experience and intuition elsewhere, eg, dot_product() being much faster than a looped sum.  Maybe there's something fishy going on with multiply.

Bob, can you check if this holds true for just a*b vs multiply(a,b)?  I'd like to know if it's Eigen being excessively clever with lazy evaluation with the sum or what.

Memory access patterns could be at play but I'm hard pressed to believe that this is what's happening here.  One possibility is that there is excessive bounds checking happening inside multiply.  That could definitely kill performance but that would depend on how things were compiled.  Can you run things again with -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG ?

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Apr 13, 2015 at 1:50 AM Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I've been doing some careful evaluations for the paper on Stan's
> autodiff and realized that for two matrices of type Matrix<var, Dynamic, Dynamic>,
> that Eigen's built-in operator*(a,b) is about 50% faster for autodiff
> than Stan's custom stan::agrad::multiply(a,b) function!
>
> I'm attaching plots of time taken relative to Stan for pretty much all
> the other open-source, operator overloading C++ autodiff packages and
> for just calling the functions with double arguments.
>

> --
> You received this message because you are subscribed to the Google Groups "stan development mailing list" group.
> To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to stan-dev+u...@googlegroups.com.
> For more options, visit https://groups.google.com/d/optout.
>
>
> I ran everything twice and the results are stable (each size is evaluated
> 2000 times for each system).
>
> The horizontal axis is total number of elements in two matrices
> a and b of type Matrix<var, Dynamic, Dynamic>.  So the biggest eval, with
> almost 2^12 (4096 or so) variables is multiplying two
> (45 x 45) matrices.  The functions being evaluated (and autodiffed for
> gradients) are:
>
>    eigen:  (a * b).sum()
>
>    stan:   sum(multiply(a,b))
>
> The operator*() and .sum() operations are built into Eigen, whereas
> the sum() and multiply() operations are from stan::agrad.
> For systems other than Stan, the Eigen version is used in both graphs.
>
> I imagine what's going on is that Eigen is very clever about
> using the traits defined in std::numeric_limits<stan::agrad::var>
> to increase memory locality by doing blocking operations.
> In all other evaluations, CppAD was slower than Adept, but here
> CppAD is a win because it also defines numeric_limits.
>
> Maybe we should just be calling Eigen's operator*() for multiplying two var
> matrices, though it'll probably take about 30--50% or so more memory.  Our
> implementation of multiply() reduces the number of vari instances, each of
> which have 16 additional bytes of overhead for a vtable pointer and adjoint,
> for an additional cost of something like 32 * (N^3 - N^2) bytes for using
> Eigen's operator*().
>
> Of course, we can't just call Eigen for var * double versions, and we
> don't exactly do a lot of matrix-matrix products of parameters, so it's
> probably no big deal.  Just a bit embarassing for the paper!
>
> - Bob
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] includes to get normal_log working?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Sorry I didn't respond right away. I could have saved you some headache.

1) stan/math/rev.hpp only includes everything in the rev folder. It doesn't arrange them in the right order. It doesn't include stan/math/prim.hpp, which it needs to do most of its stuff. It's just a catch-all.
2) I think we should be exposing header files that includes things in the right order. I've mentioned this before and I can do this, I just need help with naming. We have at least a few that I want to create:
- the Stan math library (all of it), but this is just for primitive
- the Stan math library with just scalars
- the Stan math library with scalars and matrix
- the Stan math library with scalars and array
- the Stan reverse mode library (all of it)
- the Stan reverse mode library with just scalar arguments
- the Stan reverse mode library with scalar and matrix
- the Stan reverse mode library with scalar and array

The reason we're getting order dependence is due to our traits being split up. In the order you included it, some of the traits were instantiated before the template specialization that was necessary to make it work correctly. If you look at model header, this is how we include things:

    #include <stan/math/prim/arr/meta.hpp>
    #include <stan/math/prim/mat/meta.hpp>
    #include <stan/math/prim/scal/meta.hpp>
    #include <stan/math/rev/scal/meta.hpp>
    #include <stan/math/prim.hpp>
    #include <stan/math/rev.hpp>

The important thing is that we include the meta.hpp in that order so we instantiate traits in the right order. I'm not sure there's a clean way around it. We just need to provide headers that have these template metaprograms included in the right order.

Thoughts?

Daniel

>
> So if I get rid of the above include and just use

> #include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>
>
> then it works.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: RStan vs. Stan (+ bonus on backward compatiblity)
messages.subject_clean: RStan vs. Stan (+ bonus on backward compatiblity)
messages.body_plain:
I couldn't get a word in edgewise at that meeting to clarify
what I meant.

What I was trying to say is that I don't think of things that
are only in RStan as being part of Stan.  This is purely semantic.
I'm not trying to discourage you guys from putting things into
RStan.

What I would like to encourage is that we take functionality and
put them into the C++ API for Stan --- that's what I think of as
Stan itself.  The advantage is that then we can expose them beyond
the subset of Stan users who go through RStan.  It will also save
us from having to reimplement them multiple times.

I would also like to encourage the RStan developers to keep
backward compatiblity in mind.  It's really a pain in the ass
for a user when interfaces change and the result is that users
will continue to use old versions of the system with interfaces they
know rather than switching.

I was speaking to a heavy user of JAGS who didn't want to try
Stan because he'd built up so much infrastructure around JAGS.
Changing interfaces pulls the rug out from under that kind of
infrastructure building and is really frustrating for users.

Now having said that, I do realize we have to occassionally break
backwards compatibility in the interest of making everything
better.  I just think we should do this absolutely no more than
once every couple years.  We should not under any circumstances
think of this as something that happens every couple of months as
we trickle out new features that break old things.

- Bob

I think it would be better to have a new block with a new name. The things in generated quantities get evaluated once per iteration, while the things in the unnamed block get evaluated once using all the results from all the iterations (e.g. calculating a WAIC, doing importance weighting, etc.). And I suppose they need to get written to a separate output file.

> I don't think this has anything to do with fiddling with
> functions in R, which is why I was so confused during the
> meeting.  (I also thinking changing the name from "testify"
> would be helpful for those of us who take names too literally.)

I originally envisioned it was just for testing the self-written Stan functions. But people seem to want to use it in ways that blur the distinction between Stan and the interface, so it does need a new name.

But that is also why having a new block might not even be sufficient because people will want to do things that they don't realize they want to do until later. I think calling a user-written Stan function from the interface is fine, but there is really no avoiding the looping. It is just a question of whether you do it in the interface and call a function every iteration of the loop or call the function once and loop through all the simulations in C++.

> The only reason we can't do this very easily is that we have
> no way of taking the CSV-formatted draws from CmdStan or the extracted
> draws from RStan or whatever you get out of PyStan and
> passing them back in.

I agree it is hard in general. It is not super hard with RStan and user-written functions. If you can extract() to a vector or matrix of simulations, that is easy to pass back to a user-written Stan function. What is harder is when you have a covariance matrix or something and extract() makes that into a multidimensional array. You would have to pass it back as a R list of matrices I think to be compatible with a matrix[] in the signature of your function.

Ben

Trying to extract specific structured data from the fit object to pass into
user-defined functions will be a pain in the ass, whether it’s done on
the interface level or internal to the API (the implementation of which
already makes me sad).

But why not just have a new type of Stan program instead of just
a new block?  Something like

parameters {
  … list all of the model parameters here;
}

postprocess {
  … code that gets applied to each sample;
}

Then this can be called from the interfaces via

stan.postprocess(fit_object);

Internally we read in the fit object, parse it into the original parameters
(the stan_csv_reader has methods that do much of this already), check
that the parameters are the same as those defined in this new program,
then just loop over the samples.

Something new will have to be compiled and the user will have to type
the parameters block twice but I think that is an absolutely minimal
burden compared to benefits internally.

On Wednesday, April 15, 2015 at 4:05:59 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >
> > I basically agree with this, although we currently have approximately zero known users of the C++ API
>
> False.  Just because they don’t clog the users list doesn’t mean that
> they’re not out there using the code.  For some reason they just don’t
> like to publicize their projects unless you’re meeting them in person.

That is not inconsistent with there being approximately zero known users of the C++ API relative to the huge number of known users of one of the interfaces. I'm sure there would be more API users if our API were better or more stable but still dwarfed by the number of users who don't perceive the C++ at all.

> > and from the user's perspective Stan "is" the interface that they are using.
>
> But is that interface R or Python?  PyStan has a huge number of users
> judging by the PyPI stats, and random functions developed for RStan
> will not be available to those users.

or MatlabStan or JuliaStan or StataStan ... I'm sure Stan "is" different things to different people depending on which interface they use. And I think there is consensus on trying to make the interfaces all implement low-hanging fruit, while at the same time doing what is natural within the high-level language. But there are plenty of things that weren't low-hanging fruit like ShinyStan or exposing user-defined Stan functions to the interface that I personally don't know how to do outside of R and don't personally know of anyone who knows how to do it outside of R.

> >  The C++ API should have a way to represent missingness like every other statistical software.
>
> Maybe the C++ API should do crappy inference like every other
> statistical software, too?

I don't think there is anything crappy about the way other statistical software _represents_ missingness.

> sum(is.na(poll$Income))
[1] 53

I have 53 missing values on income in this poll and the first few are

> head(which(is.na(poll$Income)))
[1]  33  42  88 207 371 576

That is totally reasonable behavior. Even Stata's 27 ways to represent missingness I can live with because I don't need the 27 largest floating point numbers anyway.

But Stata (and most software that I know of) differs from R in the default way it handles variables with missingness. If you ask for the mean of such a variable in R, it will return NA by default but there is an option to most functions that defaults to FALSE which allows you to do the calculating excluding the missing values, which is the default behavior in Stata and SPSS and whatnot. That is a design choice but not a good one because it encourages people to ignore missingness rather than modeling it. And Stan achieves the same bad behavior by not even having a convenient way to represent missingness.

> If there were a simple way to incorporate
> unknown missingness into our statically compiled models we would
> have done it by now.  Even specific missingness patterns (missing
> covariates only, for example) would be nontrivial to implement.

Depending on how you define compiled, BUGS did it 20 years ago and a Java implementation of BART does it today.  It would be simple to do in Stan for continuous data if there were a way to represent missingness. It would be simple to do in Stan for PMFs with a finite number of categories if there were a way to represent missingness.

We have quiet and signaling NaNs available in C++ but no way to do I / O with them currently. We can do the I / O with plus or minus infinity even though there are few reasons to do so, and I think they would be more usefully interpreted as missing values. Rcpp uses the R way of representing missingness but that doesn't help with the other interfaces. Maybe the simplest thing for Stan is to go the Stata route and reserve the largest numbers to represent missingness.

But there isn't going to be any development of Stan features to model missingness until there is something that a user can conveniently "if, else" on.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 15, 2015, at 1:58 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I think it would be better to have a new block with a new name. The things in generated quantities get evaluated once per iteration, while the things in the unnamed block get evaluated once using all the results from all the iterations (e.g. calculating a WAIC, doing importance weighting, etc.). And I suppose they need to get written to a separate output file.

There are actually 2 different ideas floating around here.  The first idea is to have a function, or generated quantities block, that does a certain action separately on each posterior simulation draw.  The idea is to pass it a posterior-fit Stan object with 1000 (say) draws, and it will return 1000 sets of this output.

The second idea is to do operations on all the draws together.  This is needed for EP, importance weighting, WAIC, and, for that matter, R-hat.  I hadn’t been thinking about doing the second idea in Stan but maybe it would make sense?  It would require a different sort of notation.

Also related is to allow iteration number and chain number as arguments in the model block or in the generated quantities block.

A

messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev]

I don't want to burden the users with our design discussions.
The ones who care can subscribe to stan-dev.

> On Apr 16, 2015, at 5:55 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> Following on the discussion on "testify"

I'd really like to change that nomenclature.

> which resulted in a planned delayed generated quantitiy block as far as I understood. Here is why I think you could reconsider this more in a direction of "testify":

The reason we don't want to push everything into the interfaces
is that we then have to implement everything we want five different
times or have the interfaces go without.   I'm also concerned about
testing and stability, which is much easier to just do once with
lightweight interfaces.

> Quite a number of scientific software is written as a mix of languages, i.e. a very successfull model is to code most of data handling/fiddling/processing/whatever thing in something "light" like R or Python. Then the hard stuff should always be done in something like C++.

Absolutely.  Even what people think of as pure R really
calls C++ or Fortran on the back end.

> At least this is how I have done much of my research. Following this approach means that Stan should opt to make possibly all those tremendous functionality in Stan not only available in those few blocks, but rather it should be the goal to bridge Stan space with the interface space.

I'm a bit confused by what you mean by bridging here.  I want to
build those bridges rather than having Stan be minimal with a bunch
of duplicated effort across the interfaces.

>
> This is a bit contrary to the current approach "keep the interfaces lean and let the C++ Stan handle" - but only in some sense. What would be awesome to have at some point is to tie all those Stan function into the interfaces you have, i.e. I would find it extremely helpful to just straight be abel to call lkj densities from R.

The C++ for them is there for the taking.

> Of course, not all interfaces are as rich as others, but then languages like R are so powerful that not making use of this would be a pitty. Just an example, with the current testify stuff I can define a Stan functions, which, say, takes the two parameters a and b as argument. Then having the function in R space allows me to do stuff like
>
> testify("model.stan") which has "real calc_stuff(real a, real b) {}"
>
> # also assume we have a fit
>
> post <- extract(fit, c("a", "b"))
>
> do.call(Vectorize(calc_stuff), post)
>
> Now, the last call is likely awkward looking for anyone not programming R for a while, but it is a nice example of how easy some things are in R, i.e. I get almost for free a mechanism to do posterior simulations in a very straightforward way.

Despite Andrew saying he agrees, I think this is where he disagrees.
My understanding is that he explicitly doesn't want to fiddle with
indices, either implicitly or with this kind of functional programming
in R.

I was the one saying it wasn't such a pain just to post-process R!

Andrew wanted something like Jounni's RV package --- that is, the
ability to deal with the draws in a sample without having to worry
about indexing.  So he wants to be able to take

  fit <- stan(...);

and NOT have to do

  theta <- extract(fit)$theta

and then have to do

  theta_sq <- c();
  for (n in 1:length(theta))
    theta_sq[n] <- theta[n]^2.

But rather be able to do

  fit <- stan(...)

  ... some magic happens ...

  theta_sq <- theta^2

> And one more argument for blending Stan into the interfaces - each of us is best in commanding with the interfaces the objects we care about. Hence, fitting Stan tightly into the user environment is a huge step.

Agreed.

I think we want to do the heavy lifting in Stan, though.
For instance, split R-hat and n_eff calcs are being duplicated
in the interfaces (I think), but they should be defined and
thoroughly tested in the C++ core of Stan and then wrapped by
the interfaces.

> I am speaking here as a user, of course. Software wise, I think there are approaches as Swig which goes beyond R (for R we have the wonderful Rcpp) which may we worth to consider.

We couldn't figure out SWIG and it looks like much of its
functionality is still experimental.  Rcpp can't deal with
templating, so it's rather limiting from the C++ point of view!
And we have to use inline for dynamic linking because it's purely
static.   So it should perhaps better be called Rc!

Rcpp has also been the main bottleneck in installing RStan.  Lots
of people have just given up because of the pain, or simply haven't
updated Stan in a year because it was so painful the first time.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Yes, I was not sure where to place this mail - users or dev. Since I wrote as a user, I choose user.

I see your point about the difficulty of blending Stan into language with maybe SWIG or whatever else. But how about interface specific plugins into stanc? That way stanc could create possibly multiple versions of the stan model which serve different purposes. In short, instead of having the current testify function have to mess around with the C++ code, why not extend stanc interface specific to R such that it can output a special C++ model which is easy to Rcpp it into R?

The same can likely be done for Python, I suppose. This would be an intermediate solution, I think, and it should be maintainable. The big win here is that you are then free to make use of more feature rich interfaces like R and Python in comparison to, for example, the command line.

Best,
Sebastian

> > At least this is how I have done much of my research. Following this approach means that Stan should opt to make possibly all those tremendous functionality in Stan not only available in those few blocks, but rather it should be the goal to bridge Stan space with the interface space.
>
> I'm a bit confused by what you mean by bridging here.  I want to
> build those bridges rather than having Stan be minimal with a bunch
> of duplicated effort across the interfaces.
>
> >
> > This is a bit contrary to the current approach "keep the interfaces lean and let the C++ Stan handle" - but only in some sense. What would be awesome to have at some point is to tie all those Stan function into the interfaces you have, i.e. I would find it extremely helpful to just straight be abel to call lkj densities from R.
>
> The C++ for them is there for the taking.
>
> > Of course, not all interfaces are as rich as others, but then languages like R are so powerful that not making use of this would be a pitty. Just an example, with the current testify stuff I can define a Stan functions, which, say, takes the two parameters a and b as argument. Then having the function in R space allows me to do stuff like
> >
> > testify("model.stan") which has "real calc_stuff(real a, real b) {}"
> >
> > # also assume we have a fit
> >
> > post <- extract(fit, c("a", "b"))
> >
> > do.call(Vectorize(calc_stuff), post)
> >
> > Now, the last call is likely awkward looking for anyone not programming R for a while, but it is a nice example of how easy some things are in R, i.e. I get almost for free a mechanism to do posterior simulations in a very straightforward way.
>
> Despite Andrew saying he agrees, I think this is where he disagrees.
> My understanding is that he explicitly doesn't want to fiddle with
> indices, either implicitly or with this kind of functional programming
> in R.
>
> I was the one saying it wasn't such a pain just to post-process R!
>
> Andrew wanted something like Jounni's RV package --- that is, the
> ability to deal with the draws in a sample without having to worry
> about indexing.  So he wants to be able to take
>
>   fit <- stan(...);
>
> and NOT have to do
>
>   theta <- extract(fit)$theta
>
> and then have to do
>
>   theta_sq <- c();
>   for (n in 1:length(theta))
>     theta_sq[n] <- theta[n]^2.
>
> But rather be able to do
>
>   fit <- stan(...)
>
>   ... some magic happens ...
>
>   theta_sq <- theta^2
>
> > And one more argument for blending Stan into the interfaces - each of us is best in commanding with the interfaces the objects we care about. Hence, fitting Stan tightly into the user environment is a huge step.
>
> Agreed.
>
> I think we want to do the heavy lifting in Stan, though.
> For instance, split R-hat and n_eff calcs are being duplicated
> in the interfaces (I think), but they should be defined and
> thoroughly tested in the C++ core of Stan and then wrapped by
> the interfaces.
>
> > I am speaking here as a user, of course. Software wise, I think there are approaches as Swig which goes beyond R (for R we have the wonderful Rcpp) which may we worth to consider.
>
> We couldn't figure out SWIG and it looks like much of its
> functionality is still experimental.  Rcpp can't deal with
> templating, so it's rather limiting from the C++ point of view!
> And we have to use inline for dynamic linking because it's purely
> static.   So it should perhaps better be called Rc!
>
> Rcpp has also been the main bottleneck in installing RStan.  Lots
> of people have just given up because of the pain, or simply haven't
> updated Stan in a year because it was so painful the first time.
>
> - Bob

If there is a way which avoids the use of "sourceCpp" that would even be better. The trouble with sourceCpp is that the compiled objects cannot be serialized which forces me to recompile each time I restart R. No idea what else is easily doable, but I just would like to serialize and reload instead of recompiling.

... but if a sourceCpp is the quick solution, I live with it happily and maybe this can be changed later...

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
Hey Daniel,

What seems to be the problem with the installation? Should be as simple
as "make && make install".

My problem was just when to do the linking correctly according to stan
rules. I guess rstan should do it, but all other derived packages should
know about CVODE as well. I couldn't link it into the stan library
(which now also doesn't exist anymore it seems).

As a side-note, definitely not all ODEs are stiff and the real problem
might be in the model itself (but stan shouldn't silently fail here).
Runga-kutta 45 is a good solver for a lot of problems, but the
implementation in boost is just not stable. CVODE on the other hand is
tried and proven. If people worry about the cost of an implicit solver,
CVODE also includes an explicit one and it is possible for an implicit
solver to take huge steps and still outperform a simple explicit solver.
Just my 2 cents...

Regards,
Tom

messages.subject: something for Stan that would be very useful for EP
messages.subject_clean: something for Stan that would be very useful for EP
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I’ve been thinking a lot about EP lately, and I realized that there’s something that’s currently possible but not easy to do in Stan, that I think might be worth implementing so users can do it a more automatic and natural way.

What I want is to be able to put a multivariate normal, or maybe multivariate t, prior on all the parameters of the model, all on the unconstrained scale and all concatenated into a long vector.  To do this now is possible, but it requires doing the transformations and concatenation “by hand” in the model.  Since Stan is working with this big concatenated object anyway, it would be convenient to be able to work with it directly.

The other thing I want to be able to do is to work with this concatenated vector in the postprocessing, as for EP we will need to compute its mean and covariance matrix.

Oh, and one more thing, while we’re on the topic:  Sometimes we’re doing importance weighting and we want to compute weighted means, weighted variances, and weighted cov matrix.  These are just the usual formulas, with the difference that, instead of taking averages, we take weighted averages with prespecified weights.  When all the weights are equal, it reduces to the simple mean, var, and cov matrix, with the minor difference that it’s N, not N-1, in the denominator of the var and cov (which is just the way it is; it’s not worth bothering to try to get this adjustment in).

A

P.S.  I’d be happy to also put this on Github if you tell me where it goes, but I thought this would be worth sharing with the list in any case.

messages.body_plain:
Presumably you want to add some kind of likelihood, too?
Will that just be distributions for data so that there's no
Jacobian adjustment required for the constraining transform?

If so, this probably won't be so hard --- we replace the default
uniform on the unconstrained params with a multivariate normal or
Student-t and then turn off the Jacobian.

The only trick would be specifying the prior parameters.  And of
course plumbing this through the sampler.

We're also going to be exposing the transforms, so another way to
go would be to have this, which is what you have to do now:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] mu_theta_raw;
  cov_matrix[N] Sigma_theta_raw;
parameters {
  vector[N] theta_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
  ... define params theta in terms of theta_raw using transforms ...
}
model {
  theta_raw ~ multi_normal(mu_theta_raw, Sigma_theta_raw);

  ... likelihood ...
}

But it's still going to be ugly because of slicing theta_raw into
segments.

- Bob

On Saturday, April 18, 2015 at 12:20:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If so, this probably won't be so hard --- we replace the default
> uniform on the unconstrained params with a multivariate normal or
> Student-t and then turn off the Jacobian.

I think Alp is essentially doing this now, albeit perhaps not in the most direct way. I'm doing this by hand for a conference in a couple of weeks:
z is a K-vector with iid standard normal priors and L has an lkj_corr_cholesky(1) prior
x = L * z is multivariate normal transformed parameter with marginal mean zero and unit variance but correlation matrix L * L'
p_k = Phi(x[k]) is a marginally standard uniform transformed parameter
theta_k = F_k^{-1}(p_k) is a transformed parameter with CDF F_k()

This is basically a Gaussian copula with marginal distributions that are given by your substantive prior beliefs about each theta_k.

But if the covariance matrix of the multivariate normal is unknown, then doing this multivariate Matt trick is probably a better default. Also, I need to implement more inverse CDFs.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Ben is spot on. The fullrank ADVI algorithm is closely related to gaussian EP. At a high level, here is the difference:

ADVI: min KL (q_fullrank_gaussian || posterior)

EP: min local-KL (posterior || q_fullrank_gaussian)

where "local KL" means that we only treat one component of the posterior at a time (via the tilted distribution.)

That being said, I think Andrew is asking for something different. In ADVI we automatically construct a fullrank Gaussian in the unconstrained parameter space. But we don't use it as a "prior". Actually now that I re-read it, I'm not quite sure I understand what Andrew is asking for.

Cheers
Alp
